summary: Considers the problems of downgrading X.400 (1988) messages to X.400 (1984) form. The formal rules for downgrading in X.419 were not sufficient for good service, so this document discusses further handling. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: X.400 (1988) can carry features that X.400 (1984) cannot represent. This memo describes how gateways can adapt addresses, message fields, and body parts when mail moves to an older system.

subtitle: Guidance for converting X.400 (1988) messages and addresses for X.400 (1984) systems.

tldr.problem: The X.419 downgrade rules did not cover all issues when X.400 (1988) and X.400 (1984) systems coexist.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds address mappings and describes options for downgrading message headers and body parts.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1328 is Historic; its guidance covers how the Internet and COSINE communities addressed mixed-version mail.

today: RFC 1328 is Historic. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Downgrading Is Needed
sections.content:
The RFC considers conversion from X.400 (1988) to X.400 (1984). Because the 1988 version is a strict superset of the 1984 version, the mapping problem runs in one direction. The memo extends downgrade rules in X.419 for environments containing both versions.

It recommends configuring systems to minimize downgrading and strongly advises against using 1984 systems to interconnect 1988 systems. Mixed-recipient distribution lists may use only features available to the older recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: An older mail system cannot represent every feature of the newer one. The memo explains how gateways can handle that gap and recommends avoiding downgrades where possible.

sections.title: Mapping X.400 Addresses
sections.content:
Addresses using 1988-specific features may not be representable in 1984 systems. The general method puts an encoded address in the domain-defined attribute X400-88, using the encoding described in RFC 1327. If the generated address exceeds 128 characters, the RFC allows overflow attributes X400-C1, X400-C2, and X400-C3.

A special mapping converts a common name to the Common domain-defined attribute. That downgrade works, but reverse mapping is not always possible, so cooperating 1988 systems must understand the equivalence.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway can put a newer address form into a named field the older system can carry. Some mappings cannot be reversed reliably.

sections.title: Message and Body-Part Changes
sections.content:
For message transfer, the RFC says X.419's rules are sufficient except for addressing. For an IPM downgrade from content type 22 to 2, the gateway removes 1988-specific headings, downgrades addresses, and may show a directory name as text in the Free Form Name.

Body parts may be converted without loss, converted with loss, replaced by a text explanation, or cause the message to be bounced. The choice depends on the conversion policy and destination. The RFC also allows encapsulation as a Nationally Defined 1984 body part when configured for the recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway may remove headings the older system cannot read and choose how to handle an unsupported attachment. It can convert, replace with a note, or return the message.

references.text: Kille, S., "Mapping between X.400(1988) / ISO 10021 and RFC 822", RFC 1327, May 1992.
Crocker, D., "Standard of the Format of ARPA Internet Text Messages", RFC 822, August 1982.
